## Projects

### AI Workspace for Non-Developers
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/ai-workspace
Source file: frontend/content/projects/ai-workspace.md
---
id: "02"
order: 2
slug: ai-workspace
year: "2026"
title: "AI Workspace for Non-Developers"
cardTitle: "AI Workspace"
subtitle: "For Non-Developers"
role: "Solo Developer"
category: "Personal · AI · Open Source"
description: "An open-source AI workspace for people who are not developers. An orchestrator leads a team of AI roles, and you accept only work that a check has proven."
image: "/images/projects/featured/ai-workspace.png"
tech: [Go, Svelte, Docker, MCP]
productUrl: "https://workspace.masihawam.com"
repoUrl: "https://github.com/farismnrr/agentic-ai-workspace"
---

## The problem

AI can now build and fix software for someone who cannot read code. What that person cannot do is check the result.
When the AI says "it works", they either believe it or skip the tool.

I built AI Workspace so nobody has to take the AI's word for it. Every result comes with checks that the server ran itself.

## How a request flows

You describe what you need in plain language. The workspace sizes the job, plans it when it is big, builds it step by step, and shows proof before you accept anything.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Request] --> S{Size the job}
    S -->|Small| D[Developer]
    S -->|Larger| P[Research and plan]
    P --> Y[Your yes]
    Y --> D
    D --> C[Security, QA and review]
    C --> F[Proof]
    F --> A[Accept or ask for changes]
```

## The team

Work is split across ten roles. An orchestrator leads, and each specialist has its own instructions, its own access, and optionally its own model.

| Role | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Orchestrator | Talks to you, sizes the job, plans, and hands out work |
| Researcher | Looks up facts, with sources, before anyone builds |
| Business Analyst | Turns the request into requirements and a definition of done |
| Planner | Asks you what it needs and writes the PRD |
| Architect | Designs the approach and later checks the final code against it |
| Designer | Sets the visual direction and builds the interface |
| Developer | Writes and changes the code |
| Security | Audits the code before an app is started |
| QA Tester | Runs the checks and tries to break the work |
| Reviewer | Looks at the running screens as someone who did not build them |

## Why the lead cannot edit files

The orchestrator reads files, plans, asks you questions, and delegates. It is never offered a tool that edits files or runs commands, and the server rejects the call if it tries one.
Even a one-line fix goes to the Developer, so the role that decides is never the role that does the work.

## How a job is handed over

The lead gives a teammate a role and a written brief. The teammate sees only that brief, works in its own loop, and ends with a report.
Each handoff appears as a card in your thread, so you can see who was asked and what came back.
Teammates cannot hand work on to anyone else, and only the lead can finish the task.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Lead
    participant S as Server
    participant T as Teammate
    L->>S: Delegate a job with a brief
    S->>S: Check the gates
    S->>T: Start with the brief only
    T->>S: Edits and checks
    T->>S: Report
    S->>L: Report plus what the server recorded
```

## Checks the server runs itself

A teammate's report is only what it says it did.
So the server adds what it recorded on its own: which files that role changed and which checks it ran.
The lead weighs the claim against those facts.

The proof screen works the same way. It counts only checks the server ran after the last change. Anything the AI says it checked on its own is shown as claimed and never counts.

## Gates the server enforces

A rule that lives only in a prompt can be skipped. On a real run, the research step was skipped exactly that way, so the rules that matter are enforced in code.

| Gate | What the server enforces |
| --- | --- |
| Plan approval | Nobody who builds can start until you say "Start building" on the PRD |
| Research first | The Researcher runs before the Planner, and again on the PRD's stack before anyone builds |
| Security | An app with code does not start until Security has reported on the latest changes |
| Architect | The task cannot finish until the Architect has checked the final code |
| Reviewer | When screens changed, the task cannot finish until someone else has looked at them running |
| Running app | A built page with no running app holds the finish |

Each gate allows only a few rounds. A reviewer that keeps finding things cannot stop a task from ending.

## Sizing a job

Every handoff costs time and tokens, so the lead sizes a request before it brings in the team. A question gets an answer. A small change goes straight to the Developer.
Anything new or risky runs in order: research, requirements, the PRD, design, building in slices, a styling pass, and then checks by Security, QA, the Architect, and the Reviewer.

## Long runs

The lead and its teammates draw from one budget of model turns and time, and each handoff has a smaller cap of its own. Running out pauses the task, and Continue picks up where it stopped.
If several jobs in a row change nothing and run no check, the lead is told it is stuck instead of looping.
When the context window fills, the model writes its own summary of the request, the decisions, the files touched, the open problems, and the next step.
A project also runs one task at a time, so two agents never edit the same folder.

## Safety

A role that reads text from the web cannot write files or run commands, because that text comes from strangers.
Work runs in a throwaway container with no network except a controlled proxy, and every edit keeps what was there before, so Undo restores it.

## Connecting other AI apps

Other AI apps, such as ChatGPT, can connect and work in their own project. The workspace signs them in with its own OAuth server.
You switch individual abilities on or off, and every call is logged.

## Known limits

Whoever controls the Docker socket controls the host, so the docs recommend rootless Docker.
The sandbox does not cover disk quotas or the kernel that every container shares.
A team costs more time and tokens than a single agent, which is why the lead sizes a job first.

## Links

- Product: [workspace.masihawam.com](https://workspace.masihawam.com)
- Source: [github.com/farismnrr/agentic-ai-workspace](https://github.com/farismnrr/agentic-ai-workspace)

### AskIn: AI Workspace
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/askin
Source file: frontend/content/projects/askin.md
---
id: "09"
order: 9
slug: askin
year: "2024"
title: "AskIn: AI Workspace"
cardTitle: "AskIn"
subtitle: "AI chat workspace"
role: "Backend · Integration"
category: "Ruangguru Academy · Learning Project"
description: "An AI chat app adapted from an open-source base during Ruangguru Academy: authenticated APIs, model discovery and routing, and deployment."
image: "/images/projects/askin/showcase.png"
tech: [Python, FastAPI, Svelte, TypeScript, Ollama, OpenAI API, RAG, Docker]
productUrl: ""
repoUrl: "https://github.com/farismnrr/askin"
---
## What it is

AskIn is an AI chat app I worked on during Ruangguru Academy.
It lets a user pick a model, start a conversation, add files or other context, and get an answer, without knowing which service is behind it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User] --> UI[AskIn workspace]
    UI --> CHAT[Conversation request]
    CHAT --> CONTEXT[Optional files and retrieved context]
    CONTEXT --> ROUTER[Model integration layer]
    ROUTER --> MODEL[AI model provider]
    MODEL --> RESPONSE[Generated response]
    RESPONSE --> UI
```

## How it works

The app is a customized version of an open-source chat interface (Open WebUI), with a Svelte frontend and a Python backend on FastAPI. I did not write the interface from scratch.

The backend sits between the web app and the models.
It exposes the APIs, handles authenticated requests, discovers the available models, and routes chat requests to Ollama-compatible or OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so the experience stays the same when the model changes.

It also has a retrieval step.
Files and knowledge sources can be processed into context, and relevant parts are attached to a conversation before the request reaches the model.
Requests that do not need context go through the same flow without it.

## What I worked on

My focus was the backend and the integration: understanding the architecture well enough to adapt it, run it, and reason about where the app ends and the AI services begin.
I also worked on how the app is presented, such as the new-chat screen and model selection.
Docker packaging lets the frontend and backend run as one application.

## Links

- Source: [github.com/farismnrr/askin](https://github.com/farismnrr/askin)

### GiziLens: A Team Capstone Around Food Recognition
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/gizilens
Source file: frontend/content/projects/gizilens.md
---
id: "10"
order: 10
slug: gizilens
year: "2025"
title: "GiziLens: A Team Capstone Around Food Recognition"
cardTitle: "GiziLens"
subtitle: "Team capstone: food recognition"
role: "Web & Backend Engineering · Team Capstone"
category: "DBS Foundation · Capstone Project"
description: "A DBS Foundation team capstone. One side of the team built a food-image classifier. I built the web app around it: accounts, sessions, database, and deployment."
image: "/images/projects/gizi-lens/GiziLens-showcase.png"
tech: [TypeScript, Bun, Hapi, Nuxt, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, Nginx, TensorFlow]
productUrl: ""
repoUrl: "https://github.com/orgs/Group-CC25-CF047/repositories"
---
## What it was

GiziLens was a team capstone in the DBS Foundation program. The idea: a nutrition app that starts from something users already have, a photo of food or an ingredient.

The team split in two.
One side built the food-image recognition, and the other built the web application around it: accounts, sessions, data, and deployment.
They lived in separate repositories and were not fully connected end to end, so I describe each part for what it is.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IDEA[GiziLens idea]
    IDEA --> ML[Food recognition]
    IDEA --> APP[Web application]
    ML --> CLASSIFY[Ingredient classification]
    APP --> AUTH[Accounts and sessions]
    APP --> DATA[Persistence]
    APP --> RUNTIME[Deployment]
```

## What another team member built

The classifier recognizes 32 food and ingredient classes using TensorFlow and EfficientNetV2L. The repository history attributes that work to another team member, not to me.

## What I built

I built the web application and its runtime, in a Nuxt frontend and a Bun and TypeScript backend on Hapi.

- **Authentication as a full lifecycle.** Registration for different roles, login, reading and updating the user, logout, account deletion and restore, and token refresh. JWTs protect routes, and persisted sessions let the server validate and revoke access.
- **Storage.** PostgreSQL for users and sessions, Redis as a fast-access layer, both behind repository layers instead of being called from every handler.
- **Running as a service.** Separate container builds for frontend and backend, composed with PostgreSQL, Redis, and Nginx on one Docker network, plus HTTPS setup and update scripts.
- **The logo.** I designed the original vector identity: a G, a circular lens or plate, and a leaf, with variants and usage rules.

The frontend covers registration, login, token refresh, logout, and a dashboard. It does not include the image-upload-to-classification flow, so I do not describe it as done.

## Links

- Source: [GiziLens repositories](https://github.com/orgs/Group-CC25-CF047/repositories)

### IoTNet: IoT Operations Platform
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/iotnet
Source file: frontend/content/projects/iotnet.md
---
id: "05"
order: 5
slug: iotnet
year: "2026"
title: "IoTNet: IoT Operations Platform"
cardTitle: "IoTNet"
subtitle: "IoT management platform"
role: "Solo Developer"
category: "IoT · Platform"
description: "Manage devices, users, automations, and telemetry in one place."
image: "/images/projects/iotnet/cover.png"
tech: [Nuxt, Vue, TypeScript, Hapi, Bun, PostgreSQL, MQTT, EMQX, OpenTelemetry]
productUrl: "https://i-ot.net/"
repoUrl: ""
---
## What it is

IoTNet manages devices, users, automations, and telemetry in one place. I built it alone. It sits between people and connected hardware, so users work with devices and rules instead of broker topics and raw messages.

## A command is not a result

A user asks for an outcome. The platform checks who is asking and which device it targets, publishes the command, and then waits for the device to report its state before it shows the change.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> IntentReceived
    IntentReceived --> Authorized
    Authorized --> CommandPublished
    CommandPublished --> WaitingForDevice
    WaitingForDevice --> StateObserved
    StateObserved --> ReflectedToUser
    ReflectedToUser --> [*]
```

HTTP serves the people using the app. MQTT carries the device traffic, because messages arrive asynchronously and connections come and go. The backend sits between the two.

## Ownership and automation

Every device belongs to a scope such as a tenant, an organization, or a site. Before a command goes out, the platform checks what the device can do and whether the user may ask for it.

Automations use one small model: an event, a condition, a decision, and an action.
A temperature reading can be the event, occupancy and thresholds the conditions, and the matching rule decides whether to act.
The same model covers alerts, schedules, and environment control.

## Stack

Nuxt and Vue on the front end. A TypeScript backend on Hapi and Bun, PostgreSQL for application data, MQTT through EMQX for devices, and OpenTelemetry for tracing.

## Links

- Product: [i-ot.net](https://i-ot.net/)

id: "03"
order: 3
slug: masih-awam-lms
year: "2026"
title: "Masih Awam LMS: Game-Based Learning Platform"
cardTitle: "Masih Awam LMS"
subtitle: "Game-Based Learning Platform"
role: "Backend"
category: "Learning · Rust"
description: "A learning platform where courses become worlds, quests, and lessons."
image: "/images/projects/featured/masih-awam-lms.png"
tech: [Rust, Axum, PostgreSQL, HTML, SCSS, JavaScript, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus]
productUrl: ""
repoUrl: ""
---
## What it is

A learning platform where courses become worlds, quests, and lessons. A normal course list tells you what exists. This one tries to tell the learner what to do next.

The learning structure stays familiar: courses, modules, lessons. The learner moves through worlds, quests, and checkpoints instead of a flat catalog.

```mermaid
journey
    title A learner moves through a world
    section Discover
      Enter a learning world: 5: Learner
      Understand the current quest: 4: Learner
    section Learn
      Complete a lesson: 4: Learner
      Reach a checkpoint: 5: Learner
    section Progress
      See progress update: 5: Learner
      Unlock the next stage: 5: Learner
```

## How it is built

Progress is simple on purpose: completed lessons divided by total lessons, at the lesson, quest, world, and overall level.
The story gives context for why the next lesson matters, but it never decides what counts as complete.

The product keeps three layers apart.
The experience layer holds worlds, quests, and scenes.
The learning domain holds courses, modules, lessons, and enrollment.
The progress state records what the learner actually finished.
Story and presentation can change without touching completion.

Pages are rendered according to who owns their data. Public course pages are prerendered, a learner's dashboard is rendered privately on the server, and interactive state stays in the browser.

## Stack

A Rust backend with Axum and PostgreSQL, a lightweight browser interface, and observability through OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, and Grafana.

### Multi-Tenant User Management Service
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/multitenant-user-management
Source file: frontend/content/projects/multitenant-user-management.md
---
id: "06"
order: 6
slug: multitenant-user-management
year: "2026"
title: "Multi-Tenant User Management Service"
cardTitle: "User Management"
subtitle: "Authentication and Tenant Identity Service"
role: "Solo Developer"
category: "Backend · Security"
description: "A reusable login service: one account can belong to several tenants, with a different role in each."
image: "/images/projects/user-management/cover.png"
tech: [Rust, Actix-web, PostgreSQL, RocksDB, JWT, Argon2, Docker]
productUrl: ""
repoUrl: "https://github.com/farismnrr/Multitenant-User-Management-Service"
---
## What it is

A login and identity service that several applications can share. I built it alone.

One person has one account, and that account can belong to several tenants with a different role in each.
Someone can be an admin in one organization and a normal user in another, with the same password and the same session logic everywhere.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    ACCOUNT ||--o{ TENANT_MEMBERSHIP : has
    TENANT ||--o{ TENANT_MEMBERSHIP : contains
    TENANT_MEMBERSHIP ||--o{ ROLE_ASSIGNMENT : receives
    ROLE ||--o{ ROLE_ASSIGNMENT : defines
```

## Why it is separate

When every application keeps its own users table, the same person ends up with several accounts and several role schemes, and each application handles sessions a little differently.
One service gives all of them the same answers.

## How sign-in and permissions work

Signing in proves who you are and loads your memberships. What you may do depends on the tenant you act in.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant App
    participant Identity as Identity service
    participant DB

    User->>App: Sign in
    App->>Identity: Authenticate
    Identity->>DB: Load account and memberships
    DB-->>Identity: Identity, tenants, roles
    Identity-->>App: Session and claims
    App-->>User: Authorized experience
```

Every protected action follows the same chain: identity, tenant, membership, role, permission, then allow or deny. A valid login alone never grants access.

## Tradeoffs

Applications now depend on the identity service being available. Tenant boundaries have to stay explicit everywhere, because accounts are shared. A rich role model covers more cases, but it needs discipline to stay readable.

## Stack

Rust with Actix-web, PostgreSQL for identity data, RocksDB for local caching, JWT sessions, Argon2 for password hashing, and Docker for packaging.

## Links

- Source: [github.com/farismnrr/Multitenant-User-Management-Service](https://github.com/farismnrr/Multitenant-User-Management-Service)

### Parentify: Parenting Companion
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/parentify
Source file: frontend/content/projects/parentify.md
---
id: "08"
order: 8
slug: parentify
year: "Nov — Dec 2023"
title: "Parentify: Parenting Companion"
cardTitle: "Parentify"
subtitle: "Parenting guidance and food recognition"
role: "Cloud · Backend"
category: "Bangkit Capstone · Cross-functional"
description: "A Bangkit capstone: an Android app for parenting guidance and food recognition. I worked on the cloud and backend side."
image: "/images/projects/parentify/showcase.png"
tech: [Google Cloud, Node.js, Express, MySQL, JWT, Kotlin, Android, CameraX, Retrofit, Room, Hilt, Firebase Auth, TensorFlow, Keras, TensorFlow Lite]
productUrl: ""
repoUrl: "https://github.com/orgs/Parentify/repositories"
---
## What it was

Parentify was our Bangkit Academy capstone: an Android app that puts parenting guidance and camera-based food recognition in one place. A parent can read articles, or photograph an ingredient and get information about it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Parent] --> APP[Parentify Android app]
    APP --> GUIDE[Parenting guidance]
    APP --> CAMERA[Capture food image]
    GUIDE --> API[Application API]
    CAMERA --> MODEL[Food classifier]
    API --> DATA[Parenting and food data]
    MODEL --> RESULT[Detected ingredient]
    RESULT --> DATA
    DATA --> APP
```

## The three tracks

- **Mobile Development** built the Android client in Kotlin, with camera capture and local storage.
- **Cloud Computing** built the backend API, authentication, application data, and the contract the app depends on.
- **Machine Learning** trained a convolutional network to classify 36 food-ingredient categories and exported it for mobile use. The best validation accuracy in the recorded experiment was about 93.7%. That is a training result, not a promise for real camera input.

## What I built

I was on the Cloud Computing track.
I built the backend the Android app talks to: a Node.js service on Express for authentication, parenting articles, and food information, with MySQL for the data.
Sign-in used JWTs and bcrypt password hashing, and requests were validated with Joi.

The backend was prepared for Google Cloud with deployment notes and an update script, and Postman documentation helped the three teams test the API contract.
That contract mattered most: each team could work on its own only because names, payloads, and data relationships matched.

## Links

- [Cloud Computing](https://github.com/Parentify/Parentify-Cloud-Computing): backend API, data, and cloud setup.
- [Mobile Development](https://github.com/Parentify/Parentify-Mobile-Development): the Android app.
- [Machine Learning](https://github.com/Parentify/Parentify-Machine-Learning): dataset workflow and model training.

### Personal Portfolio Website
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/portfolio-website
Source file: frontend/content/projects/portfolio-website.md
---
id: "07"
order: 7
slug: portfolio-website
year: "2026"
title: "Personal Portfolio Website"
cardTitle: "Portfolio"
subtitle: "Markdown-driven portfolio"
role: "Solo Developer"
category: "Web · Portfolio"
description: "This site. Projects, experience, and certifications are Markdown files, not hardcoded UI data."
image: "/images/projects/portfolio/cover.png"
tech: [Svelte 5, Vite, TypeScript, Markdown, Mermaid, Rust, Axum, GitHub Actions]
productUrl: "https://farismnrr.com"
repoUrl: "https://github.com/farismnrr/portofolio"
---
## What it is

This site.
Projects, experience, certifications, and blog posts are Markdown files, and one content collection drives every view: the project list, the home page, and each detail page.
Adding a project means writing a file, not editing a component.

## How it is built

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[Markdown collections] --> B[Build process]
    S[Svelte UI] --> B
    B --> P[Prerendered route HTML]
    B --> A[Static assets]
    P --> R[Rust + Axum runtime]
    A --> R
    R --> U[Visitor]
```

Public routes are prerendered at build time, so crawlers and browsers get real HTML right away.
Svelte then hydrates the page for client-side navigation.
A small Rust and Axum server embeds the generated pages and assets for production.

The site keeps ordinary web behavior: normal link handling, lazy route loading, hash links that wait for the page before scrolling, separate desktop and mobile navigation, and a skip link to the main content.

## Tradeoffs

Markdown is comfortable for me and works well with Git history, but it is harder for non-technical editors.
Content changes are versioned and reviewable, but they still need a build and a deployment.
Every project can tell a different story, so a writing check in the build keeps the copy consistent.

## Stack

Svelte 5 and Vite, Markdown with Mermaid for diagrams, prerendering at build time, Rust with Axum in production, and GitHub Actions for validation, build, and deployment.

## Links

- Site: [farismnrr.com](https://farismnrr.com)
- Source: [github.com/farismnrr/portofolio](https://github.com/farismnrr/portofolio)

## What it is

Sensio IoT lets people control a room: lights, temperature, and equipment, with sensor readings and automation in one view. A team builds it across application engineering, device integration, infrastructure, security, and UI/UX.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Choose a room] --> V[Review controls and readings]
    V --> A[Request an action]
    A --> F[Follow the feedback]
```

## What I worked on

I build the backend side: commands, device-state feedback, and permissions.

- **Request and result are separate.** Sending a command is not the same as the device changing, so the app keeps the requested action apart from the state the device reports, and the interface shows what actually happened.
- **Clear feedback when a device is unavailable.** An interruption produces an understandable message instead of an action that looks finished.
- **Permissions on controls.** Users see which actions they may take, and get a useful reason when one cannot be completed.

I also test, troubleshoot with the device engineers, and work with the infrastructure and security engineers on releases.

## Links

- Product: [sensio.id](https://sensio.id)

### Sensio Notes: Meeting Intelligence Platform
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/projects/sensio-notes
Source file: frontend/content/projects/sensio-notes.md
---
id: "01"
order: 1
slug: sensio-notes
year: "2026"
title: "Sensio Notes: Meeting Intelligence Platform"
cardTitle: "Sensio Notes"
subtitle: "Meeting assistant"
role: "Fullstack"
category: "PT Perkasa Pilar Utama · Product Development"
description: "A meeting assistant that turns recordings into summaries and action items. I worked on recording, upload, and progress."
image: "/images/projects/sensio-notes/showcase.png"
tech: [Backend Development, Web Applications, Mobile Integration, Application Reliability]
productUrl: "https://sensio.id"
repoUrl: ""
---
## What it is

Sensio Notes records or imports a meeting and turns it into a summary, decisions, and action items you can search later.
I work on it as part of a team with AI, infrastructure, security, and UI/UX engineers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Record or upload a meeting] --> P[Follow progress]
    P --> V[Review meeting results]
    V --> F[Find decisions and follow-up work]
```

## What I worked on

My part is getting a recording into the system safely and keeping the user informed until the results are ready.

- **Uploads that survive a bad connection.** Recordings over 100 MB are sent in parts. After a dropped connection, the upload continues from the last finished part, and retries respect the server's backoff.
- **No lost meetings.** An in-progress recording is backed up locally on web and mobile, so a crash or a closed tab does not lose it.
- **Progress and errors people can read.** The interface separates work that is continuing, work that needs attention, and results that are ready, and it keeps web and mobile behavior consistent.

I also take part in testing, diagnosing production issues, and releases. The AI features are built by other members of the team.

## Links

- Product: [sensio.id](https://sensio.id)

### Building IoTNet: What Changed When Devices Became a Fleet
Canonical: https://farismnrr.com/blog/building-iotnet
Source file: frontend/content/blog/building-iotnet.md
---
slug: building-iotnet
title: "Building IoTNet: What Changed When Devices Became a Fleet"
excerpt: "Notes on the architecture decisions behind IoTNet, especially identity, device state, MQTT, automation, and the gap between sending a command and knowing what happened."
category: Engineering
published: 2026-01-12
readTime: 5 min read
cover: /images/blog/iot-mesh-networks-1280.webp
featured: true
---

## The Problem Changed with Scale

A single connected device is mostly an integration problem. A fleet is an operations problem.

Once more users and devices share the same platform, the difficult questions move away from the protocol itself.

The system has to know who owns a device, who may control it, how current state is represented, and what should happen when hardware disappears from the network.

That shift is what shaped IoTNet.

## A Command Is Not a State Change

One of the most useful distinctions in the platform is between requesting an action and observing the result.

When a user clicks a control, the application can validate the request and publish a command. That only proves that the platform attempted the action. It does not prove that the physical device changed state.

The useful flow is closer to this:

```text
user intent
→ authorization
→ command publish
→ device execution
→ state or telemetry update
→ UI reflects observed state
```

That extra step matters in IoT because networks fail, devices restart, brokers reconnect, and hardware does not always behave like an in-memory object.

## Why HTTP and MQTT Have Different Jobs

I do not try to force user workflows and device communication through the same transport model.

HTTP works well for application actions such as signing in, loading resources, changing configuration, or asking the platform to perform an operation. MQTT is better suited to devices that publish state asynchronously and may disconnect without warning.

In IoTNet, the conceptual boundary is simple:

```text
human workflow → application API
device workflow → broker messaging
```

The backend sits between those two sides. It turns product-level requests into device-level messages and turns incoming device events back into application state.

## Identity Became Part of the Device Model

Device control stopped being only a messaging problem as soon as more than one user or organization shared the platform.

Before a command reaches a device, the backend needs enough context to answer questions such as:

- Which tenant or organization owns this device?
- Is this user allowed to operate it?
- Which target should receive the command?
- Should this user be able to see the returned state?

That is why I treat identity, ownership, and device messaging as connected parts of the same system rather than separate features added later.

## Automation Works Better as Small Building Blocks

The automation model is intentionally plain:

```text
event
→ condition
→ decision
→ action
```

The value comes from keeping those stages explicit.

A temperature update can become an event. Occupancy or a threshold can become a condition. The rule decides whether anything should happen, and only then does the platform dispatch an action.

This keeps the automation engine easier to inspect when a rule behaves unexpectedly. It also makes different use cases share the same model instead of growing a new feature path for every device type.

## The Platform Is a Coordination Layer

The architecture is easier to reason about when the platform owns product meaning and the broker owns message delivery.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U[User] --> API[Application API]
    API --> AUTH[Identity and access]
    API --> RULES[Rules and automation]
    RULES --> MQTT[MQTT / EMQX]
    API --> MQTT
    MQTT --> DEV[Connected devices]
    DEV --> MQTT
    MQTT --> STATE[State and telemetry handling]
    STATE --> API
    API --> U
```

That separation gives each layer a clearer responsibility. The application decides what an action means and whether it is allowed. The messaging layer moves commands and events. Device state is then folded back into the product model.

## What Became Harder Than Expected

The difficult parts were not the ones that look impressive in a demo.

Keeping state understandable after reconnects was harder than sending a command. Access boundaries mattered more as soon as multiple users shared the same environment. Automation needed enough flexibility to be useful without becoming impossible to predict.

Observability also became more important as the system grew. When a device, broker, API request, or background process can all be part of one user-visible failure, logs and traces are not optional debugging extras. They are how the failure path becomes visible.

## What I Would Keep If I Rebuilt It

I would keep the same high-level boundaries:

1. Keep user-facing API work separate from device messaging.
2. Treat authorization as part of every device action, not a frontend concern.
3. Distinguish a published command from an observed device state.
4. Keep automation rules explicit enough to inspect after the fact.
5. Add observability early, before the number of integrations makes failures difficult to trace.

The individual frameworks can change. Those boundaries are more durable than the stack around them.

## Current Stack

The current platform uses Nuxt and Vue on the frontend, a TypeScript backend with Hapi and Bun, PostgreSQL for application data, MQTT with EMQX for device messaging, and OpenTelemetry for operational visibility.

The project page has the broader product and system overview: [IoTNet](/projects/iotnet).

**Live product:** [i-ot.net](https://i-ot.net/)
